intro_line: Three AI stories worth knowing about today, in under a minute.

stories.headline: Z.ai unveils open coding model to rival Claude
bullets: GLM-5.3 is built for coding, with weights due within two weeks.
Z.ai says it scores close to Claude Fable 5 on coding tasks.
A permissive licence could let teams self-host it far more cheaply.
stories.original_title: Z.ai to Rival Anthropic, OpenAI in Coding With New AI Model
stories.summary: Z.ai announced GLM-5.3, an upgraded coding-focused model built on the same roughly 700-billion-parameter base as GLM-5.2. Weights are due within two weeks under a permissive licence.
stories.script_line: Chinese lab Z.ai has unveiled GLM-5.3, a coding model it says performs close to Claude. The weights are due within two weeks under a permissive licence, so teams could self-host it cheaply.
stories.why_it_matters: Strong coding models may stop being something you can only rent from a US lab.

stories.headline: OpenAI runs GPT-5.6 up to 14x faster
bullets: Ultrafast mode reaches up to 750 output tokens per second.
It is an API preview for selected customers, widening as capacity grows.
stories.original_title: Previewing Ultrafast mode: GPT-5.6 Sol at up to 14X the speed
stories.summary: OpenAI previewed Ultrafast mode for GPT-5.6 Sol, running up to 14 times faster and generating up to 750 output tokens per second. It launched in limited preview to a select group of API customers on 13 August 2026.
stories.script_line: OpenAI is previewing Ultrafast mode, running GPT-5.6 Sol up to fourteen times faster, at up to seven hundred and fifty tokens a second. It's a limited API preview for now.
stories.why_it_matters: AI assistants and voice agents can start to feel genuinely instant.

stories.headline: UK courts ban Meta smart glasses
bullets: Courts and tribunals across England and Wales barred the wearables.
The concern is that recording is hard for anyone nearby to notice.
Points to tighter rules ahead for AI wearables in public places.
stories.original_title: England and Wales ban Meta Glasses from courtrooms
stories.summary: His Majesty's Courts & Tribunals Service has prohibited Meta smart glasses from courtrooms in England and Wales, citing the difficulty of detecting when the devices are recording.
stories.script_line: And in the UK, courts and tribunals in England and Wales have banned Meta's smart glasses, because it's hard to tell when they're recording.
stories.why_it_matters: Expect more venues to restrict AI wearables before the law catches up.

matters_professionals: Faster inference and open coding models widen what you can ship this quarter.
matters_businesses: Cheap self-hosted models and new wearable rules both land on this year's roadmap.
matters_learners: Open-weight releases are the cheapest way to practise on frontier-class models.
